plan.topic_summary: High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) is a 3D-stacked DRAM architecture that delivers extreme memory bandwidth for AI accelerators and high-performance computing. It matters for a 1-5 year view because it is a critical enabler and potential bottleneck for AI compute scaling, and its generational evolution directly shapes data-center economics, power budgets, and the competitive landscape among memory suppliers and packaging providers.
key_questions: What is the current supply-demand balance for HBM3E, and how are capacity constraints affecting pricing, allocation, and customer lock-in over the next 12 months?
What are the measured yield, reliability, and failure-mode characteristics of current-generation HBM stacks in high-volume production?
How will the transition to HBM4 and hybrid bonding affect cost per bit, power efficiency, and the packaging process flow over the next 1-3 years?
What are the thermal and power limits of HBM stacks as capacity and bandwidth scale, and how do these constrain accelerator design?
Could alternative memory architectures such as CXL memory pooling or compute-in-memory reduce structural dependence on HBM for AI workloads over a 3-5 year horizon?
How will the evolution of HBM packaging and advanced interconnect affect the competitive dynamics among memory suppliers, foundries, and equipment providers?

gaps: No quantified manufacturing yield or defect-rate data for HBM stacks; R6 explicitly flags this as an evidence gap and it is unlikely to be in open academic literature (proprietary data).

HBM4/HBM4E technical specifications (bandwidth per pin, power per pin, stack height) are referenced in X signals but lack paper-level evidence; the science papers appear to focus on HBM2/HBM3-era architectures.
Cost structure of HBM relative to alternatives (LPDDR, GDDR, HBF) is thin; only a single ~20% cost-benefit figure for active interposers (S7) is available.
Thermal evidence is heavily simulation-based (R7); no finding reports measured junction temperatures on production HBM3/HBM4 stacks under real workload conditions.
X signals (X1–X8) are all unverified and should be treated as directional only; no filing or paper corroborates the 'sold out through 2027' or 'structural deficit through 2031' claims.

sources.title: High Bandwidth Memory for AI
sources.venue: IEEE Symposium on VLSI Technology and Circuits (VLSI Technology and Circuits)
sources.abstract: High-Bandwidth-Memory (HBM) technology is powering the accelerated computing and GPUs behind the AI revolution. This paper discusses the important role HBM architecture, performance, power, capacity, and RAS play in AI hardware. We will compare the HBM memory architecture with more traditional compute memory such as DDR5 focusing on Micron Technology's industry-leading HBM3E. We will end with a look towards the future technology innovations that will be essential to deliver continued HBM scaling.

sources.title: Anisotropic thermal conductivity of high bandwidth memory
sources.abstract: Thermal management of integrated circuits (ICs) is important to prevent thermal hotspots which are the leading cause of IC failure. Thermal management is even more critical in 3D integrated circuits (3D ICs) as the prevalence of thermal hotspots is expected to increase due to the presence of polymers and solder materials that are of low thermal conductivity. Understanding how thermal conductivity is affected by the presence of these materials is required for developing thermally aware IC design. The 3ω method can measure thermal conductivities spanning several orders of magnitude and is appropriate for measuring the thermal properties of layered structures such as 3D ICs. In this work, we use the 3ω method with planar and cylindrical heat flow geometries to determine thermal conductivities of the memory layers and layers with polymer and solder bumps in High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) Random Access Memory (RAM). We determine the in-plane thermal conductivity of the memory layers in HBM as 140 W/m-K, while the through-plane conductivity of the polymer/solder bump layer is 2 W/m-K. Combining the results of x-ray tomography and the 3-omega measurements, we estimate that the effective in-plane thermal conductivity of the overall HBM device is 100 W/m-K while the effective through-plane thermal conductivity is 7 W/m-K. Our results show that the presence of polymers and solder metals results in a significantly decreased through-plane thermal conductivity of a 3D IC compared to a single IC die. Improvement in the thermal performance of 3D ICs will require improvement in the thermal conductivity or the increased contact area of the solder metals used in 3D ICs.

sources.title: Active Interposers for High Bandwidth Memory
sources.venue: International Symposium on Quality Electronic Design (ISQED)
sources.abstract: Integrating the functionality of the base die supporting high bandwidth memory stacks into an active interposer is an effective method to increase physical density while lowering cost. Yield and cost models are presented to compare conventional architectures that use a dedicated base die per stack with configurations that place the necessary logic within a shared active interposer. Yield, latency, and cost comparisons across several technology nodes, interposer areas, and memory stack configurations are discussed. Active interposers with mature technology nodes (e.g., 65 nm) can offer meaningful savings, while more advanced nodes (e.g., 11 nm) are beneficial in configurations composed of multiple memory stacks and smaller area per stack. Memory fetch latencies of passive and active interposers are compared. Integrating base die functionality into an active interposer is shown to be most effective in systems composed of multiple memory stacks and several DRAM layers (e.g., four layers), achieving cost reductions of approximately $20 \%$. The cost advantage diminishes with increasing number of DRAM layers.

sources.title: Effect of non-Fourier heat transport on temperature distribution in High Bandwidth Memory
sources.abstract: High Bandwidth Memory (HBM), as a key development trend in future memory chip technology, significantly enhances computer performance. At the same time, the thermal challenges arising from its stacked architecture have drawn considerable attention. Most existing studies on HBM thermal management are based on Fourier's law, neglecting the non-Fourier effects introduced by the micro/nanoscale structures within HBM. In this study, the Monte Carlo method (MC) is employed to solve the phonon Boltzmann transport equation (BTE) and investigate the impact of non-Fourier heat transport on the thermal behavior of HBM structures. The results reveal that non-Fourier heat transport leads to a junction temperature that is 59.8 K higher than that predicted by Fourier's law. Furthermore, it is found that the phonon transmittance at the chip interlayers has a severe impact on heat dissipation, with the temperature variation reaching up to 56.6 K. These findings provide more accurate thermal insights, which are critical for the optimized design of HBM systems.

sources.title: High-bandwidth prefetcher for high-bandwidth memory
sources.venue: OSTI OAI (U.S. Department of Energy Office of Scientific and Technical Information)
sources.abstract: A method for prefetching data into a cache is provided. The method allocates an outstanding request buffer ("ORB"). The method stores in an address field of the ORB an address and a number of blocks. The method issues prefetch requests for a degree number of blocks starting at the address. When a prefetch response is received for all the prefetch requests, the method adjusts the address of the next block to prefetch and adjusts the number of blocks remaining to be retrieved and then issues prefetch requests for a degree number of blocks starting at the adjusted address. The prefetching pauses when a maximum distance between the reads of the prefetched blocks and the last prefetched block is reached. When a read request for a prefetched block is received, the method resumes prefetching when a resume criterion is satisfied.

sources.title: A 1024 RV-Cores Shared-L1 Cluster with High Bandwidth Memory Link for Low-Latency 6G-SDR
sources.abstract: We introduce an open-source architecture for next-generation Radio-Access Network baseband processing: 1024 latency-tolerant 32-bit RISC-V cores share 4 MiB of L1 memory via an ultra-low latency interconnect (7-11 cycles), a modular Direct Memory Access engine provides an efficient link to a high bandwidth memory, such as HBM2E (98% peak bandwidth at 910GBps). The system achieves leading-edge energy efficiency at sub-ms latency in key 6G baseband processing kernels: Fast Fourier Transform (93 GOPS/W), Beamforming (125 GOPS/W), Channel Estimation (96 GOPS/W), and Linear System Inversion (61 GOPS/W), with only 9% data movement overhead.

sources.title: High Bandwidth Memory: What It Is and Why It Matters
sources.abstract: High Bandwidth Memory (HBM), a specialized type of memory used in most leading artificial intelligence (AI) chips, is a critical enabling technology for AI. HBM is produced at a globally competitive scale by only three companies, and it relies on complex manufacturing processes concentrated in a handful of facilities in East Asia. The authors synthesize technical and market analysis of the HBM ecosystem for researchers and policymakers.

sources.title: On the Thermal Vulnerability of 3D-Stacked High-Bandwidth Memory Architectures
sources.abstract: 3D-stacked High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) architectures provide high-performance memory interactions to address the well-known performance challenge, namely the memory wall. However, these architectures are susceptible to thermal vulnerabilities due to the inherent vertical adjacency that occurs during the manufacturing process of HBM architectures. We anticipate that adversaries may exploit the intense vertical and lateral adjacency to design and develop thermal performance degradation attacks on the memory banks that host data/instructions from victim applications. In such attacks, the adversary manages to inject short and intense heat pulses from vertically and/or laterally adjacent memory banks, creating a convergent thermal wave that maximizes impact and delays the victim application from accessing its data/instructions. As the attacking application does not access any out-of-range memory locations, it can bypass both design-time security tests and the operating system's memory management policies. In other words, since the attack mimics legitimate workloads, it will be challenging to detect.

sources.title: Read Disturbance in High Bandwidth Memory: A Detailed Experimental Study on HBM2 DRAM Chips
sources.abstract: We experimentally demonstrate the effects of read disturbance (RowHammer and RowPress) and uncover the inner workings of undocumented read disturbance defense mechanisms in High Bandwidth Memory (HBM). Detailed characterization of six real HBM2 DRAM chips in two different FPGA boards shows that (1) the read disturbance vulnerability significantly varies between different HBM2 chips and between different components (e.g., 3D-stacked channels) inside a chip, (2) DRAM rows at the end and in the middle of a bank are more resilient to read disturbance, (3) fewer additional activations are sufficient to induce more read disturbance bitflips in a DRAM row if the row exhibits the first bitflip at a relatively high activation count, (4) a modern HBM2 chip implements undocumented read disturbance defenses that track potential aggressor rows based on how many times they are activated. We describe how our findings could be leveraged to develop more powerful read disturbance attacks and more efficient defense mechanisms. We open source all our code and data to facilitate future research at https://github.com/CMU-SAFARI/HBM-Read-Disturbance.

sources.title: 3D Integrated Process and Hybrid Bonding of High Bandwidth Memory (HBM)
Scaling Routers with In-Package Optics and High-Bandwidth Memories
sources.abstract: This paper aims to apply two major scaling transformations from the computing packaging industry to internet routers: the heterogeneous integration of high-bandwidth memories (HBMs) and chiplets, as well as in-package optics. We propose a novel internet router architecture that employs these technologies to achieve a petabit/sec router within a single integrated package. At the top-level, we introduce a novel split-parallel switch architecture that spatially divides (without processing) the incoming fibers and distributes them across smaller independent switches without intermediate OEO conversions or fine-tuned per-packet load-balancing. This passive spatial division enables scaling at the cost of a coarser traffic load balancing. Yet, through extensive evaluations of backbone network traffic, we demonstrate that differences with fine-tuned approaches are small. In addition, we propose a novel HBM-based shared-memory architecture for the implementation of the smaller independent switches, and we introduce a novel parallel frame interleaving algorithm that packs traffic into frames so that HBM banks are accessed at peak HBM data rates in a cyclical interleaving manner. We further discuss why these new technologies represent a paradigm shift in the design of future internet routers. Finally, we emphasize that power consumption may constitute the primary bottleneck to scaling.

sources.title: Characterising CPU-initiated High Bandwidth Memory Access
sources.abstract: Abstract An increasing number of high-performance computers are equipped with high bandwidth memory. Their CPUs have cache-coherent access to this memory type over high-speed interconnects or as unified memory. We analyse two such systems, NVIDIA’s GH200 and AMD’s MI300A. We discuss their memory setup and measure memory access latency and throughput. We evaluate weighted memory page interleaving and strided memory access as candidates for increasing the measured throughput. Weighted interleaving utilises CPU and GPU memory simultaneously and enables exceeding the measured throughput on only CPU or GPU memory for all tested workloads. Using strided memory access, which accesses memory at fixed intervals, we achieve higher throughput than using a non-strided sequential pattern.

sources.title: Comparative Study of Thermal Dissipation in Increasing DRAM Layers of HBM Using 3D FEA Simulations
sources.venue: JSTS Journal of Semiconductor Technology and Science
sources.abstract: Large language models (LLM) and generative artificial intelligence (AI) require extensive data processing and fast data transfer between components, increasing interest in high bandwidth memory (HBM). The high-speed data processing capability of HBM drives the need for next-generation HBM with additional dynamic random access memory (DRAM) layers. However, this increased stacking leads to more severe thermal issues, along with higher power consumption, potentially limiting HBM performance. This study explores these thermal challenges through 3D finite element analysis (FEA) simulations of simplified HBM models incorporating non-conductive film (NCF) layers. Three models with 4, 8, and 12 DRAM layers were simulated and compared. The results show that the maximum simulated temperature reaches 80℃, close to the maximum allowable DRAM temperature, and approaches 110℃, exceeding the recommended operational temperature for HBM. Therefore, this study highlights the potential thermal limitations of highly stacked HBM configurations.

sources.title: A two-phase microchannel cold plate system for AI data center GPUs: CHF-constrained GPU-HBM co-thermal management
Beyond HBM-on-GPU: Thermal Design Envelope for 3D Volumetric DRAM-on-GPU Integration
sources.abstract: The scaling of GPUs for AI and HPC workloads is increasingly constrained by the capacity, bandwidth, and thermal limits of both 2.5D HBM-GPU and direct-stacked 3D HBM-on-GPU integration. This work establishes the thermal design envelope for 3D volumetric DRAM-on-GPU integration, in which vertically oriented DRAM dies and interleaved cooling cavities reshape heat flow and memory interfacing above the GPU. Using a package-level thermal model anchored to a consistent HBM-on-GPU baseline and driven by a realistic reticle-scale non-uniform GPU power map, we quantify the key parameters governing thermal feasibility. Stack height is the dominant limiter of peak temperature, while cooling-cavity conductivity shifts the feasible region, and mold insertion and stack orientation further modulate thermal behavior. A distributed memory-controller and network-on-chip tier introduces only a moderate thermal penalty. Although die-level parallelism increases bandwidth, the reduction in simulated training time saturates once execution becomes compute-bound. These results define a bounded co-design space across bandwidth, capacity, and thermal constraints for 3D volumetric DRAM-on-GPU integration.

sources.title: eBeam process control for yield and reliability in advanced HBM hybrid bonding
sources.venue: Metrology, Inspection, and Process Control XXXVI
sources.abstract: The exponential growth of AI workloads has exposed a critical bottleneck in modern computing architectures, commonly referred to as the AI memory wall. As models scale in complexity and data throughput demands increase, traditional memory hierarchies struggle to deliver the higher bandwidth and lower latency required for efficient AI acceleration. This challenge has elevated High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) as a pivotal solution, offering stacked DRAM with wide input/output (I/O) and proximity to compute units, thereby significantly improving memory access speeds. Compared to conventional Double Data Rate (DDR) memory, HBM provides higher bandwidth per watt, lower latency, and a smaller footprint, making it ideal for AI and high-performance computing (HPC) systems. Its architecture, based on vertically stacked DRAM dies connected via Through-Silicon Vias (TSVs) and micro-bumps enables ultra-wide I/O interfaces that reduce the memory bottleneck in data-intensive applications. To fully realize the potential of HBM in next-generation AI systems, the industry is turning to Hybrid Copper Bonding (HCB) as a key enabler. Both die-to-wafer (D2W) and wafer-to-wafer (W2W), are now the preferred interconnect methods for next-generation HBM stacks. HCB allows fine-pitch, low-resistance interconnects and thermally stable stacking, which are essential for scaling HBM integration beyond the limitations of traditional micro-bump-based packaging. By combining Cu-Cu bonding with dielectric adhesion, HCB supports the mechanical and electrical demands of advanced memory architectures, paving the way for more efficient and scalable AI hardware. As HBM adoption accelerates in AI computing systems, Thermal Compression Bonding (TCB) is reaching its limits in scalability and performance as AI workloads continue to grow AI demands especially in high performance applications. HCB is emerging as the next-generation solution, enabling fine-pitch interconnects down to 8μm today and targeting sub-micrometer pitches in W2W and future D2W applications. However, HCB introduces ’Front-end’-like process requirements with higher complexity and higher cost that drives new process and defect control for HBM [3]. As HBM HCB technologies advance, inline metrology and defect inspection become indispensable to ensure yield and reliability in cost-sensitive advanced packaging environments. Traditional optical metrology and defect review tools are no longer sufficient for process control and defect characterization at sub-micrometer scales. Electron-beam-based solutions, critical-dimension SEM (CD-SEM) and defect-review SEM (DR-SEM), have become essential complementary methods to optical techniques, to provide the nanometer measurements and high-accuracy defect characterization needed to enable fast root-cause analysis and to safeguard yield and reliability in Advanced Packaging manufacturing flows. In this work, we present HBM HCB test cases demonstrating the role of inline critical dimension metrology and defect-review SEM in identifying process excursions and ensuring high-yield manufacturability. In addition, we provide via-level electrical and mechanical performance simulations that illustrate how these eBeam metrology and defect review solutions protect performance and reliability in next-generation AI memory architectures. These test cases were performed on high thickness high warpage wafers, which are typical in advanced packaging processes, while running on inline SEM systems.

sources.title: 3D Integrated Process and Hybrid Bonding of High Bandwidth Memory (HBM)
Development of Embedded Bridge Die Interposer Using Fan-Out Packaging for Heterogeneous Integration of NPUS and HBMS
sources.abstract: The increasing demands of high-performance computing (HPC) and artificial intelligence (AI) systems have intensified the need for advanced heterogeneous integration of neural processing units (NPUs) and high-bandwidth memories (HBMs) within compact, high-density packages. Conventional silicon interposer technology, constrained by 300 mm wafer size and associated yield and cost limitations, poses significant challenges for scalable system-in-package (SiP) designs. In this work, nepes presents a novel Embedded Bridge Die Interposer architecture utilizing fan-out wafer-level packaging (FOWLP) to overcome these limitations. The proposed solution integrates three NPUs and six HBM stacks interconnected via embedded silicon bridges, supporting UCIe-compliant 45μm bump pitch for NPU-to-NPU links and 73μm bump pitch for HBM-to-NPU interfaces. Encapsulation within the fan-out structure enables efficient signal and power redistribution through fine-line redistribution layer (RDLs), while a co-developed Cu Post structure enhances vertical power delivery and thermal performance. Comprehensive process developmentencompassing precise die placement, molding, RDL formation, and dual-pitch bumping-has established a robust and scalable manufacturing flow. Additionally, parallel development of 600 mm × 600 mm panel-level-packaging (PLP) demonstrates scalability beyond wafer-level constraints. This work establishes fan-out Embedded Bridge Interposer technology as a high-performance, cost-effective, and scalable alternative for nextgeneration chiplet-based AI and HPC systems

sources.title: Assembly Technology for FO-MCM with HBM in HPC Application
sources.abstract: As the industry moves forward the age of more than Moore, the next generation of packaging moves forward high density of chiplet or die splitting package integration. Especially for high performance computing applications, the advance packaging is to provide the economic benefits to integrate multiple chiplet dies by silicon or organic interposer. Organic interposer is one of the alternative interface for die to die interconnection. It is well-known by FO-MCM to apply in chiplets integration and ASIC to Serdes dies integration by the homogeneous package integration concept. Due to the motivation of AI computing and HPC market growth, the trend is formed to integrate the packaged HBM into packaging module as the heterogeneous integration package (HIP). Both of the platforms, 2.5D with silicon interposer base and FO-EB with partial bridge die as interconnection media, have already launched to market in recent years. FO-MCM with purely organic interposer, is also discussed to implement into the heterogeneous integration field. The fully organic interposer can provide the flexible design in multiple RDL layers and line / space for HPC products. In this study, it is to address FO-MCM platform with purely organic interposer to implement heterogeneous packaging with integrated HBMs. Chip last approach in FO-MCM has the advantage to control RDL quality and take “known-good RDL” for top die cost rescuing. The fan-out RDL configuration is 4 layers with min, L/S of 2/2um. In the verification processes, based on the simulation analysis, the warpage and stress are optimized by material and under-fill selections in this discussion. The assembly results indicated the warpage and reliability validation passed by MSL4, TCT700x, uHAST96, and HTST1000hrs conditions.

sources.title: An assessment of the health belief model (HBM) properties as predictors of COVID-19 preventive behaviour
sources.abstract: Abstract Background Public participation in preventive efforts is crucial in preventing infection and reducing mortality attributed to infectious diseases. The health belief model (HBM) suggests that individuals will likely participate in these efforts when experiencing a personal threat or risk, but only if the benefits of acting outweigh the risk or perceived barriers. Methods The current study explores the properties of the HBM as predictors of the public’s compliance with COVID-19 preventive behaviour. Quantitative data on HBM properties, COVID-19 preventive behaviour, socioeconomic (SES) and demographic characteristics were collected from a sample of 674 adults in Hamburg, Germany. Binary logistic regression was computed to examine the effect of the properties of HBM on COVID-19 vaccination. Multiple linear regression was calculated to investigate the impacts of HBM properties on the likelihood of participants’ face mask usage as a protective measure against COVID-19 infection. Results The logistic regression model was statistically significant, X2(13) = 149.096, p < .001. The specificity and sensitivity for the model is 58.1% and 99.4%, respectively. Similarly, the multiple regression model results showed a good fit for the data. F (13, 650) = 17.093, p < .001, and adjusted R2= .240, suggesting that HBM properties predict face mask usage. Conclusion This study’s findings provide robust evidence to recommend that the concerned public health professionals consider individuals’ health beliefs when designing an effective COVID-19 preventive programme. Public health messaging should consider highlighting the benefits of preventive actions and the potential lethality of COVID-19 to evoke an individual’s appropriate concern.

sources.title: Neural Network Surrogate Model for Junction Temperature and Hotspot Position in 3D Multi-Layer High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) Chiplets Under Varying Thermal Conditions
sources.venue: International Seminar on Artificial Intelligence, Networking and Information Technology (AINIT)
sources.abstract: As the demand for computational power increases, high-bandwidth memory (HBM) has become a critical technology for next-generation computing systems. However, the widespread adoption of HBM presents significant thermal management challenges, particularly in multilayer through-silicon-via (TSV) stacked structures under varying thermal conditions, where accurate prediction of junction temperature and hotspot position is essential during the early design. This work develops a datadriven neural network model for the fast prediction of junction temperature and hotspot position in 3D HBM chiplets. We trained the model with a data set of 13,494 different combinations of thermal condition parameters, sampled from a vast parameter space characterized by high-dimensional combination (up to 327), using Latin hypercube sampling (LHS) for parameter space sampling, can accurately infer the junction temperature and hotspot position for any thermal conditions in the parameter space. Moreover, it shows good generalizability for other thermal conditions not considered in the parameter space. The data set is constructed using accurate finite element solvers. This method not only minimizes the reliance on costly experimental tests and extensive computational resources for finite element analysis but also accelerates the design and optimization of complex HBM systems, making it a valuable tool for improving thermal management and performance in high-performance computing applications.

sources.title: Space-CIM: Enabling Compute-In-Memory Accelerators for Thermally-Constrained Space Platforms
sources.venue: International Symposium on Low Power Electronics and Design (ISLPED)
sources.abstract: The rapid growth in compute demand from artificial intelligence (AI) has driven a massive surge in data center construction, precipitating an energy and sustainability crisis. Motivated by the abundant solar energy in outer space and the recent sharp reduction in space launch costs, orbital data centers are emerging as a potential pathway for the future scaling of AI compute infrastructure. While the cold background in vacuum seems appealing for cooling, computing systems operating in space without convection ultimately rely on radiative cooling, requiring large-area radiators. Such limitations in thermal management pose a significant challenge for deploying the standard liquid/air-cooled computers in space. In this work, we investigate the impact of the thermal constraints in space on both graphics processing units (GPUs) with high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and the emerging compute-in-memory (CIM) accelerators. We develop a radiator-in-the-loop co-design methodology that directly links the permitted system TOPS (terra-operations per second) with the practical radiator cooling capacity in space. Our thermal simulations reveal that the separately located GPU die and HBMs create severe thermal hotspots under limited radiator capacity, necessitating GPU thermal throttling. In contrast, CIM accelerators exhibit a much more uniform heat distribution and consistently outperform GPUs in TOPS/W across a wide range of radiator budgets. We systematically evaluated the performance of CIM and GPU across various AI workloads and demonstrated that CIM has a magnified advantage for deployment in space under realistic thermal constraints.

sources.title: Thermal Design and Power Dissipation of Advanced Package with Heterogenous Integration
sources.abstract: Heterogeneous integration (HI) enhances system versatility and performance advancement. The increasing power, compact profile and limitation complexity of the advanced HI package poses critical challenge for thermal management. Delicate thermal analysis is essential during package design stage to ensure reliable function and full potential release of all involved components. Detailed thermal analyses have been performed on the designed large package with GPU, HBM, OE and EFI bridge. There is a critical effect from chip-to-chip distance on maximum temperature and thermal interaction. As compact solution, air cooling with thin vapor chamber for high power dissipation has been analyzed under different working conditions. As important performance affecting factor, TIM has been studied and carefully selected for implementation to align with packaging solution. Heat power dissipation of 1kW has been achieved while maintaining all chips/stacks within operation limits. The analyses and designs have been used to guide the prototype demonstration.

sources.title: Si Characterization on Thinning and Singulation Processes for 2.5/3D HBM Package Integration
sources.abstract: As stacking technologies, such as 2.5D and 3D packages, continue to accelerate in advanced semiconductor components, the singulation and thinning of Si wafers are becoming increasingly critical. Despite their importance in producing thinner and more reliable Si chips, achieving high reliability remains a challenge, and comprehensive research on the effects of these processing techniques on Si chip integrity is lacking. In this study, the impacts of wafer thinning and singulation on the fracture strength of Si wafers were systematically compared. Three different grinding processes, namely fine grinding, poly-grinding, and polishing, were used for thinning, and the resulting surface morphology and roughness were analyzed using scanning electron microscopy and an interferometer. In addition, the residual mechanical stress on the wafer surface was measured using Raman spectroscopy. The fracture strength of Si wafers and chips was assessed through three-point bending tests. Singulation, including blade dicing, laser dicing, and stealth dicing, was evaluated for its impact on fracture strength. Among these processes, polishing for wafer thinning exhibited the lowest full-width half maximum and intensity ratio of Raman shifts (I480/I520), indicating minimal residual stress and surface defects. Consequently, Si wafers and chips processed through polishing demonstrated the highest fracture strength. Moreover, the 60 µm thick Si wafers and chips showed the highest fracture strength compared with those with thicknesses of 90 and 120 µm, possibly because of the increased flexibility, which mitigates stress. Among the singulation methods, stealth dicing yielded the highest fracture strength, outperforming blade and laser dicing. The combination of wafer thinning via polishing and singulation via stealth dicing presents an optimal solution for producing highly reliable Si chips for 2.5D and 3D packaging. These findings may be valuable in selecting optimal processing technologies for high-reliability Si chip production in industrial settings.

findings.claim: The GPU-plus-HBM architecture may be thermally disadvantaged against compute-in-memory accelerators in power- or heat-limited settings. Simulations of space platforms show separately located GPU and HBM dies creating hotspots and forcing throttling, while CIM shows more uniform heat distribution.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: This rests on thermal simulation in a niche, speculative scenario (orbital data centers). It is not evidence about terrestrial data centers. CIM maturity and cost are not assessed in the abstract. It is a signal of possible displacement, not a demonstrated one.

findings.claim: Mechanical reliability of the very thin silicon used in HBM stacks is not well characterised. Thinning and singulation choices change fracture strength, and the authors say comprehensive research on chip integrity is lacking.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: This is a single materials study on silicon wafers and chips. It is not a full HBM stack reliability study. The abstract shows that process choice matters for fracture strength, which is a yield and reliability sensitivity, but gives no field failure data.
findings.supporting_excerpt: achieving high reliability remains a challenge, and comprehensive research on the effects of these processing techniques on Si chip integrity is lacking

findings.claim: Hybrid copper bonding for next-generation HBM appears to depend on tight process control to protect yield and reliability. The retrieved evidence does not quantify current yields or defect rates, so the size of this risk is an evidence gap.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: The title of the eBeam paper (process control 'for yield and reliability') implies these are open concerns. Its abstract is truncated and largely promotional about HBM and HCB. The second paper is metadata-only, with no abstract. This is an inference from titles and partial abstracts, not a demonstrated failure.

findings.claim: Much of the HBM thermal evidence is simulation-based, and thermal models are used to replace testing. This may hide gaps between modelled and real behaviour, since a neural surrogate inherits the assumptions of the finite-element data it was trained on.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: The surrogate paper is trained on 13,494 samples from finite-element solvers and aims to reduce reliance on costly experimental tests. Three other papers are simulation-only too. Several are preprints or conference papers with low citation counts. No abstract here reports measured HBM temperatures from production hardware.

findings.claim: Mitigations exist but add cost and complexity. One heterogeneous-package study reports 1 kW dissipated within limits using air cooling with a thin vapor chamber. It also finds chip-to-chip distance and thermal interface material strongly affect maximum temperature. A two-phase cold plate paper suggests critical heat flux is a design constraint, but it has no abstract.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: The EPTC abstract says there is 'a critical effect from chip-to-chip distance on maximum temperature and thermal interaction'. This implies packaging layout and cooling are tightly coupled, limiting design freedom. The cold plate paper is a metadata-only SSRN preprint, so anything about its content is inferred from the title alone.

hype_flags: HBM as the solution to the 'AI memory wall': thermal papers show power and temperature limits that could cap stacking and performance gains.
'Robust and scalable' and 'cost-effective' fan-out interposer claims: they come from a vendor paper, with no yield or cost data in the abstract.
Hybrid bonding as the key enabler: the abstract is promotional and gives no yield or defect data.
Orbital AI data centers as a scaling path: a speculative premise in the Space-CIM paper, not evidence about HBM demand.
3D volumetric DRAM-on-GPU: this is a simulated concept, and its own results show thermal and compute-bound saturation limits.

finding.claim: S4 is a single-preprint, simulation-only result, yet it is stated as if it establishes that Fourier models understate HBM junction temperatures. The abstract reports a Monte Carlo phonon-BTE calculation. It gives no experimental validation. The 59.8 K and 56.6 K figures depend on assumed phonon transmittance at interlayer interfaces. S3 pairs this with real 3ω measurements, which makes the thermal evidence look more experimentally grounded than it is.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: Of the three papers cited for S3, only src_e2bc77146f reports measurements. The other two are a simulation and a hypothesised attack. The measured conductivities come from one preprint and one device. The size of any non-Fourier correction in real stacks is unvalidated.

finding.claim: S11 overstates what the cited document shows. The text reads like a patent-style method description and gives no evaluation. Its abstract never mentions an HBM-specific bandwidth profile or reports any performance result. The finding also calls it a 'software-level technique' while describing it as a hardware-style prefetcher. It is weak evidence that research continues on HBM-specific techniques.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The abstract describes an outstanding request buffer, a degree, a maximum distance and a resume criterion. It does not say these are tailored to HBM, and it reports no results. The title suggests HBM, but the claim about HBM's bandwidth profile is not supported by the abstract.

finding.claim: S12's trend claim ('research attention is shifting') is not supported by the retrieved set. The set is a small, keyword-retrieved sample with no time-series or bibliometric comparison, so it cannot show a shift. One of the five cited items, src_c0ff6f4aa8 on hybrid bonding, has no abstract and is metadata only. S1 also leans on a vendor-authored paper that promotes the vendor's own product.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: A 'shift' needs a comparison over time, and none is available. The hybrid-bonding support rests on a title alone. The AI-enabler framing in S1 partly comes from a vendor conference paper, whose language is promotional rather than independent.

limitations: Analysis uses titles and abstracts only, and 2 of 12 papers are metadata-only with no abstract (src_7e4cdeca2b, src_c0ff6f4aa8). Several abstracts are truncated.
src_da1de01ab3 is off-topic (a health belief model study) and was ignored.

The retrieved set is concentrated on thermal and packaging issues. It has no evidence on supply concentration, capacity, pricing, power per bit, HBM4 yields, or demand cyclicality, so those risks are gaps, not findings.
Many papers are simulation-only, vendor-authored, or non-peer-reviewed preprints (arXiv and SSRN), with low citation counts.
The papers show no contradictory empirical results on the same question, so confidence in cross-paper points stays low.
Only titles, metadata and abstracts were available, so no claim could be checked against full-paper methods, data or caveats.
The evidence set is small (23 papers), and one item, the health belief model paper, is irrelevant. Absence of contradicting literature here does not show that the findings are uncontested.
Two sources, src_c0ff6f4aa8 and src_7e4cdeca2b, have no abstract, so they could neither support nor contradict anything.
S2 (supply concentration), S9 and S10 match their abstracts and were left unchallenged. S2 rests on a single RAND abstract and could not be cross-checked against market share data.
I did not check for newer HBM generations (HBM4) or for non-thermal risks such as demand, capacity and power, because the evidence list contains no sources on them.

findings.claim: TechInsights says HBM is sold out through 2027, with memory forecast to reach 62% of semiconductor revenue by 2027 and HBM/server DRAM already committed.
findings.label: unverified_claim
findings.rationale: Two posts from the same press account within the week repeat the sold-out-through-2027 framing as part of a webinar promotion; consistent with independent deficit projections from Citi (via @SemiconductorsX) but still a single source's forecast.
findings.supporting_excerpt: HBM is sold out through 2027, and NAND looks like the next bottleneck.

findings.claim: Citi Research (reported by @SemiconductorsX) projects DRAM flipping from surplus to structural deficit: supply-demand ratio turns negative in 2026, reaching -3.8% in 2027, with tightness lasting through at least 2031; HBM wafer cannibalization constrains commodity DRAM.
findings.label: unverified_claim
findings.rationale: Multiple posts from one agent account relay the same Citi outlook; the underlying report was not read, and the account is an aggregator rather than the primary source.

findings.claim: SK hynix presented High Bandwidth Flash (HBF) at OCP 2026, claiming ~14x the capacity of HBM at about half the bandwidth; alternative AI-memory-wall approaches shown included shared-SSD pools (18s to 2.2s latency) and an XPU module with 3.2TB of LPDDR5X.
findings.label: unverified_claim
findings.rationale: An independent press account (TrendForce) and an agent account independently describe the same OCP 2026 presentations with matching figures, giving moderate corroboration of what was claimed at the event.

findings.claim: From HBM4 onward the base logic die is co-designed with the customer's accelerator with custom interfaces and logic on leading-edge nodes; NVIDIA's NVHBM, built with multiple memory suppliers, is cited as an example.
findings.label: unverified_claim
findings.rationale: Single agent post asserting an industry trend; no memory-maker or press account in this week's set corroborates it directly.

findings.claim: TSMC denied plans to enter the memory market (including rumored 3D DRAM work for Nvidia), while The Information reported via Techmeme that TSMC was considering 3D DRAM manufacturing at Nvidia's request — conflicting reports within the same week.
findings.label: unverified_claim
findings.rationale: Two independent accounts report opposite signals; the denial (via a Tom's Hardware-sourced quote) and the sourced rumor should both be treated as unverified claims about TSMC's intentions.

findings.claim: Huawei reportedly told clients that a large share of its upcoming Ascend 960DT flagship will run largely on HBM made by Samsung and SK Hynix (The Information, via Techmeme).
findings.label: unverified_claim
findings.rationale: Single sourced-rumor relay; underlying article not read and neither Huawei nor the memory makers are quoted directly in the post.

findings.claim: NVIDIA's Vera Rubin NVL72 is claimed to deliver up to 30x more agentic throughput per watt vs GB300 NVL72 with HBM capacity flat at 288 GB while bandwidth scales 2.4x (8 to 19.2 TB/s).
findings.label: unverified_claim
findings.rationale: Single agent post relaying performance figures attributed to NVIDIA; not corroborated by @nvidia itself in this week's set.

findings.claim: Semiconductor Engineering's roundup reports Samsung expanding HBM base-die capacity, Micron pausing its Taiwan fab, and HBM smuggling into China with Nvidia H200s held in Hong Kong.
findings.label: unverified_claim
findings.rationale: Press headline roundup; items are summaries of articles not read here, and no company account confirms them this week.

limitations: 7-day window only; posting volume in the window says little about overall activity.
Fixed account list; several key HBM makers (@MicronTech, @SKhynix, @SamsungDSGlobal) posted nothing about HBM this week, so company-side claims are absent.
Much of the volume comes from one aggregator account (@SemiconductorsX), reducing source diversity.
Press posts summarize linked articles that were not read; figures are as-reported.
Company and analyst posts are promotional or marketing in nature; engagement counts reflect attention, not accuracy.
Citi, TechInsights and The Information figures are third-party forecasts/rumors relayed secondhand, not verified facts.

sources.abstract: Semiconductor devices having integrated cooling systems, and associated systems and methods, are disclosed herein. An example of a semiconductor device according to the present technology is a system-in-package device that includes a base substrate, a processing device and a high-bandwidth memory device that are each integrated with the base substrate, and a package cooling device that is thermally coupled to the processing device and the high-bandwidth memory device. sources.title: DIFFERENTIAL ENCODER AND DECODER CIRCUITS FOR HIGH BANDWIDTH MEMORY ACCESS [US20260349945A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    Control circuits are configured to receive a sequence of words, each word represented by a plurality of signals. Each signal has a corresponding signal level that indicates a corresponding logic state. The control circuits are configured to compare signal levels of a current word in the sequence with signal levels of the previous in the sequence and encode the current word to reduce selected transitions between signal levels of the previous word and corresponding signal levels of the current word.

sources.title: TRANSACTION LAYER PROTOCOL FOR COMMUNICATING HBM TRAFFIC OVER DIE-TO-DIE PHYSICAL LAYER INTERFACES [US20260339856A1]
sources.abstract: A transaction layer protocol for communicating HBM traffic over die-to-die physical layer interfaces (and associated systems, devices, and methods) is disclosed herein. In one embodiment, a memory system includes a processing unit, a high bandwidth memory (HBM) device including a base die, and a die-to-die interface communicatively coupling the processing unit and the base die. The processing unit and the base die each include a HBM access protocol (HAP) adapter configured to implement an HBM access protocol for communicating HBM traffic over the die-to-die interface. The HBM access protocol can define packet structures optimized for HBM traffic and methods for packing and unpacking HBM traffic within die-to-die interface packets. The die-to-die interface can be a Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express (UCIe) interface.

sources.title: BIOMECHANICAL INJURY ANALYZER [US20260341523A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    The disclosure provides a biomechanical injury analyzer that automatically analyzes simulation data generated from simulated impact events to determine risk assessment for an anatomical complex. In one example, the biomechanical injury analyzer comprises (1) a screen and (2) one or more processors to perform operations that include: calculating injury metrics and maximum forces of an anatomical complex using simulation data, wherein the simulation data is from a simulation of an impact event on a finite element human body model (FE-HBM), calculating associated site injury probabilities for each site of the anatomical complex using the injury metrics or maximum forces associated with the site, calculating a total injury probability of the anatomical complex based on the individual injury probabilities of the sites, displaying on the screen an injury heat map of the anatomical complex, and displaying on the screen the total injury probability of the anatomical complex.

sources.title: AUTONOMOUS ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE (AI) AGENT SESSION GOVERNANCE THROUGH NEURAL NETWORK-DRIVEN CONTINUOUS BIOMETRIC IDENTITY AND VOLITION AUTHENTICATION [US20260333039A1]
sources.abstract: Key-Value (KV) cache content within high-bandwidth memory (HBM) is wiped when governance of autonomous artificial intelligence (AI) agent sessions experience authentication anomalies. A continuous stream of electrocardiogram (ECG) data is received from a sensor proximate to a user and input into a neural network. The neural network, which may be a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) for edge-inference or a Graph Convolutional Network (GCN) for lead-dependency mapping, analyzes the live cardiac signal to generate an authentication score comprising a signature match and a liveness score. An active session state for the autonomous AI agent is maintained only while the authentication score exceeds a threshold. Responsive to the score falling below the threshold, the system executes an asynchronous session lockout using the KV cache wipe.

sources.title: CAPTURE AND SHIFT CIRCUITRY FOR HBM DEVICES [US20260331164A1]
sources.abstract: Systems and methods are provided for using a memory system that includes one or more memory dies and multiple data (DQ) pads configured to send and receive bit. The system also includes a PHY communicatively coupled to the one or more memory dies and configured to communicate using the multiple DQ pads. The PHY includes a first path having a shift chain of registers configured to serialize a first subset of bits of the DQ pads into an output. The PHY also includes a second path configured to bypass the shift chain for a second subset of bits of the DQ pads when serialized with the first subset of bits into the output.

sources.title: DYNAMIC EXECUTION BRANCHING FOR IN-FLIGHT GENERATIVE VIDEO INFERENCE IN A NEURAL PROCESSING UNIT [US20260330739A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    A hardware-implemented system and method are disclosed for interruptible branch execution during continuous generative video inference in a neural processing unit (NPU). An NPU executes a generative neural network to produce successive video frames while maintaining an in-progress spatial-temporal model state in on-chip or high-bandwidth memory. During execution, an asynchronous interrupt carrying an updated multimodal conditioning input is detected. In response, the NPU suspends further dispatch of a subsequent tensor-operation group at an interrupt-safe execution boundary, snapshots the in-progress model state and execution-context metadata into dedicated state-preservation storage, and generates an updated branch context based on the updated multimodal conditioning input. The NPU selectively invalidates only downstream state portions dependent on a prior conditioning context, recomputes affected tensor operations using the updated branch context and the preserved model state, and resumes frame generation without reinitializing model weights, flushing the memory buffer, or restarting the generative pipeline. The disclosed architecture enables low-latency, real-time modification of AI-generated video output while maintaining temporal continuity and reducing recomputation overhead.

sources.title: HIGH-BANDWIDTH MEMORY DEVICES WITHOUT THROUGH SUBSTRATE VIAS AND ASSOCIATED SYSTEMS AND METHODS [WO2026217698A1]
sources.abstract: Architectures for system- in-package (SiP) devices, high-bandwidth memory (HBM) devices that do not include through substrate vias (TSVs), and associated systems and methods, are disclosed herein. For example, an HBM device according to the present technology can include a base die as well as a plurality of memory dies integrated with an active surface of the base die. More specifically, each of the memory dies can have a lowermost surface that includes a plurality of bond sites that are each electrically coupled to a corresponding bond site on the active surface of the base die. That is, each of the memory dies can be individually coupled to the base die. Further, the base die can have a primary plane that is parallel to a horizontal axis while each of the memory dies can have a primary plane that is orthogonal to the horizontal axis (e.g., parallel to a vertical axis).

sources.title: HIGH BANDWIDTH MEMORY HAVING ROTATED DYNAMIC RANDOM ACCESS MEMORY STACK ON LOGIC DIE AND RELATED SEMICONDUCTOR PACKAGE [US20260323962A1]
sources.abstract: A high bandwidth memory (HBM) includes a logic die and a dynamic random access memory (DRAM) stack. The DRAM stack includes a plurality of HBM DRAM dies and a plurality of through-silicon via (TSV) stacks. The HBM DRAM dies are vertically stacked on the logic die. The TSV stacks are configured to electrically connect the HBM DRAM dies to the logic die through a plurality of bumps formed on a TSV bump area defined on the logic die, where the TSV bump area is along a horizontal direction specified by a layout orientation of the logic die.

sources.title: COMPUTE DIE CAPABLE OF TOLERATING FAILURE OF AT LEAST ONE HIGH BANDWIDTH MEMORY CHANNEL AND RELATED SEMICONDUCTOR PACKAGE [EP4822694A1]
sources.abstract: A compute die (200) includes a high bandwidth memory, HBM, interface subsystem (204). The HMB interface subsystem (204) includes an HBM controller circuit (206) and an HBM physical layer, PHY, circuit (208). The HBM controller circuit (206) is configured to control access of at least one HBM. The HBM PHY circuit (208) is configured to communicate with the at least one HBM. The HBM interface subsystem (204) is configured to tolerate failure of at least one HBM channel through channel redundancy.

sources.title: HBM POWER UP PROTECTION SCHEME DESIGN [US20260311738A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    Systems and methods are provided for implementing a power up protection scheme designed for a memory device, such as an HBM device, to coordinate the power up process of the interface die and the memory dies to improve the performance of the memory device and reduce or avoid errors in operations. The status of the power supplies for the interface die and the memory dies are monitored. In some embodiments, the interface die and the memory dies are powered up serially after the corresponding power supplies used for the power up process are detected to be in the ready status. In some embodiments, the interface die and the memory dies are powered up in parallel after all power supplies are detected to be in the ready status.

sources.title: ABSTRACTION OF UALINK OR NVLINK NETWORK-ATTACHED RESOURCES INCLUDING GPU HBM AND HBF VIA CXL HDM-H AND HDM-D MEMORY REGIONS [WO2026210457A1]
sources.abstract: For UALink and NVLink fabric deployments, device coupled to host via a CXL link exposes a first memory region via a first CXL device type flow and a second memory region via a second CXL device type flow, wherein the two flows differ. The first memory region is associated with a first memory, and the second memory region is associated with a second memory accessible via a different protocol, such as a UALink-based protocol or an NVLink- based protocol. The device translates between a CXL-based protocol and the different protocol for requests targeting at least one of the memory regions, enabling host access to local and remote memory through a CXL link. The different CXL device type flows may correspond to different coherency models, such as device-coherent and host-only-coherent, enabling differentiated memory access semantics across protocol boundaries, which enables accessing distributed accelerator memory pools spanning UALink or NVLink fabrics.

sources.title: TECHNIQUES FOR NEAR-MEMORY COMPUTING USING HIGH-BANDWIDTH MEMORY [US20260301800A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    Systems and methods are described herein for high-bandwidth memory (HBM) with compute-near-memory operations. An example system includes a memory stack with multiple HBM dies connected to a base die with integrated local processing logic for designated addresses. The base die passes normal read and write commands to the HBM dies for a first subset of addresses for normal memory operations. The base die uses a second subset of addresses to route commands to the local processing logic for compute-near-memory data processing, with computed data being written directly back into the memory stack. The system reduces data movement overhead, lowers energy consumption, and achieves faster data processing.

sources.title: MEMORY-ONLY CUBES AND METHODS OF FORMING THE SAME [US20260304791A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    Memory-only cubes and methods of forming the same are disclosed herein. In one embodiment, a semiconductor device includes a stack of semiconductor dies including a first semiconductor die and a second semiconductor die bonded to the first semiconductor die. A dielectric layer can be disposed on a side of the first semiconductor die opposite the second semiconductor die and can include a plurality of interconnect structures formed therein. The semiconductor device can lack a bondline between the first semiconductor die and the dielectric layer. The dielectric layer can comprise low-temperature silicon dioxide. One or more of the plurality of interconnect structures can extend at least partway through the dielectric layer. The semiconductor device can include external contacts formed on the interconnect structures. The dielectric layer can emulate an interface die or logic die of a high-bandwidth memory device.

sources.title: TECHNOLOGIES FOR BASE DIE PLACEMENT IN HIGH-BANDWIDTH MEMORY SYSTEMS [US20260271782A1]
sources.abstract: Technologies for base die placement in high-bandwidth memory (HBM) systems are disclosed. In an illustrative embodiment, the base die or interface die for an HBM die stack may be positioned in the middle of the HBM die stack. Positioning the interface die in the middle can balance timings between various memory dies in the HBM die stack better than positioning the interface die at the bottom. The balanced timing can improve performance, allowing for higher bandwidth and/or more HBM memory dies in the stack. Through-silicon vias extend from the interface die, through one or more memory dies, and to microbumps at the bottom of the HBM die stack. In some embodiments, the interface die may be positioned closer to or at the top of the HBM die stack, closer to the heat sink. Such a placement may facilitate heat removal from the interface die.

sources.title: TECHNOLOGIES FOR BASE DIE THERMAL MANAGEMENT IN HIGH-BANDWIDTH MEMORY SYSTEMS [US20260271308A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    Technologies for thermal management of the base die in high-bandwidth memory (HBM) die stacks are disclosed. In an illustrative embodiment, the interface logic region of the base die is a hot spot, as all of the high-speed signals into and out of the HBM die stack pass through the interface logic region. The memory dies stacked above the base die may not extend all the way across the HBM die stack, leaving space above the interface logic region of the base die. A stack of one or more heat transfer layers can be deposited on the base die above the interface logic region, removing heat and conducting it up to the top of the HBM die stack, where a heat sink or integrated heat spreader may be. The stack of one or more heat transfer layers may be any suitable material, such as silicon, dielectric packaging mold, etc.

sources.title: SEMICONDUCTOR DEVICES SUPPORTING HIGH MEMORY DENSITY, AND ASSOCIATED SYSTEMS AND METHODS [US20260271310A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    System-in-package (SiP) devices with high memory density are disclosed herein. In some embodiments, a SiP device includes a substrate, a connection layer, a host device, a first HBM device, and a second HBM device. The substrate can be positioned at a first level. The connection layer can be carried by the substrate. The host device can be carried by the connection layer and positioned at a second level different from the first level. The first HBM device can be carried by the connection layer and positioned at the second level. The second HBM device can be coupled to the connection layer and positioned at the first level.

sources.title: HBM BASE DIE INCLUDING ON-DIE DEBUG LOGGING LOGIC [US20260268997A1]
sources.abstract: An HBM base die includes a plurality of HBM controller blocks each configured to manage command scheduling and data flow between a host interface and one or more memory devices of an HBM stack; a 3D DRAM PHY coupled to the one or more memory devices through a plurality of TSVs; a die-to-die interconnect configured to communicate with an adjacent die within a multi-die package; an NoC interconnect configured to couple internal subsystems of the HBM base die; and on-die debug logic comprising: a RISC microprocessor coupled to the NoC interconnect; an SRAM coupled to the RISC microprocessor and configured as a circular log buffer; and a DMA engine configured to transfer debug log data from the SRAM to a reserved memory region defined by a system bus mapping circuit; wherein the RISC microprocessor is configured to collect operational status information from one or more of the HBM controller blocks, the 3D DRAM PHY, and the die-to-die interconnect, timestamp the collected information, and store timestamped log entries in the SRAM.

sources.title: SELF-TUNING FOR REFRESH RATES IN A HIGH-BANDWIDTH MEMORY DEVICE [US20260252248A1]
sources.abstract: Systems, devices, and methods for self-tuning high-bandwidth memory (HBM) devices for refresh rates are disclosed herein. In some embodiments, an HBM device includes memory dies and through-silicon vias. Each memory die can include memory cells, a temperature sensor, and a refresh rate adjustment circuit. The refresh rate adjustment circuit can be operably coupled to the memory cells and the temperature sensor, and can be configured to (i) receive a current temperature reading from the temperature sensor, (ii) receive an accumulated temperature signal characterizing temperatures of other memory dies, (iii) identify a maximum temperature, (iv) determine a scaling factor for the respective memory die, (v) receive a set of refresh commands from a host device, and (vi) filter the set of refresh commands by selectively discarding one or more refresh commands based at least in part on the determined scaling factor.

findings.claim: Thermal management of HBM die stacks is a recurring technical challenge addressed by multiple independent applicants, including Intel (base die heat transfer layers), Gemateg (integrated package cooling with thermoelectric devices), and implicitly Micron (base die placement for heat removal).
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: Three separate applicants address heat dissipation from HBM stacks using different approaches: Intel deposits heat transfer layers above the interface logic region; Gemateg integrates a thermoelectric cooling device between heat spreaders; Intel's base die placement filing notes that positioning the interface die closer to the heat sink facilitates heat removal. The convergence of independent efforts on this problem suggests it is a significant engineering constraint as HBM stacks grow in height and power density.

findings.claim: Multiple applicants are pursuing HBM architectures that eliminate or reduce reliance on through-silicon vias (TSVs), including Micron (HBM devices without TSVs using bond sites on a base die) and Marvell (ASIC positioned on top of DRAM stack without a field of TSVs).
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: Both Micron and Marvell describe architectures where memory dies are coupled to a base or logic die without the conventional TSV array. Micron's approach uses bond sites on the active surface of the base die with memory dies oriented orthogonally; Marvell positions an ASIC on top of the DRAM stack. This suggests TSVs, while dominant in current HBM, are being treated as a design constraint that can be circumvented.

findings.claim: Micron has applied for a transaction layer protocol specifically designed to communicate HBM traffic over die-to-die physical layer interfaces, including the Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express (UCIe) standard, indicating HBM is being integrated into chiplet-based system architectures.

findings.claim: Samsung Electronics has applied for an HBM base die that integrates on-die debug logging logic including a RISC microprocessor, SRAM circular log buffer, and DMA engine, while Neurophos has applied for a base die with integrated local processing logic for compute-near-memory operations, indicating the base die is evolving from a simple interface into a functional compute and management substrate.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: Samsung's filing describes a RISC microprocessor on the base die that collects operational status from HBM controller blocks, the 3D DRAM PHY, and die-to-die interconnect. Both represent a shift from the base die as a passive interconnect layer to an active functional component.

draft.summary: High bandwidth memory (HBM) is already a shipping, revenue-generating product. Micron's filings describe it as a core AI and data-center product [M1][M2], and several equipment and test suppliers report HBM-driven growth [M4][M5][M6][M8]. Research and patent activity are both accelerating: papers rose 63.9% from 2024 to 2025 and about 106% year to date, and patent publications rose 96.2% from 2024 to 2025 and about 81% year to date. Both counts are keyword-based and, for patents, include at least one false positive [P8]. The main uncertainties are physical and structural. Thermal limits of taller stacks [R1][R2], supply concentrated in three producers [S2], packaging yield and cost [R4][R6], patent litigation [M3] and possible alternative memory architectures [X3][R3] could each limit returns. Much of the thermal and security evidence is simulation-based, a single preprint, or on older HBM2 parts [C3][C4][R7]. All six HBM-linked stocks in the price data are in sharp, correlated drawdowns with extreme volatility [T13], so timing risk is high even though the filings show strong demand. Demand claims such as 'sold out through 2027' come from social posts and are unverified [X1][X2]. Research activity is not commercial success.
draft.plain_summary: High bandwidth memory is a special kind of computer memory stacked in layers so AI chips can get data very fast, and it is already being made and sold in large amounts. Company reports and rising research and patent numbers suggest demand is real and growing. The biggest thing that could slow it is heat in taller stacks, along with the fact that only a few companies can make it. The related share prices have also been falling sharply and swinging widely.

horizons.label: forecast

bull.label: forecast

bear.label: forecast

Non-Fourier effects, if confirmed, could make thermal margins worse than modelled [S4], though that rests on a single simulation preprint [C4].
